title: 21 Ideas for Developing the Motivational Character Strengths
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. follows up an earlier post on the four and a half motivational character strengths with a practical catalogue of classroom moves for building grit's passion component, purpose, curiosity, gratitude and optimism. He argues that for many students passion is still nascent, so the teacher's job is to help them tell mere affinities from interests worth developing. Several ideas are his own, notably the brief one-on-one affirmation of a student's observed strength, which he describes as forty seconds of work that can yield forty years of results, and the distinction between fruitful and fruitless curiosity. Others are drawn, with attribution, from Character Lab, such as gratitude notes, asking students what kind of person they want to be, and specific rather than global negative feedback. A footnote explains why grit counts as half a motivational strength: passion is the motivational element, while persistence is its product.
points: Stuart holds that motivating oneself is a learnable part of flourishing and that teachers can help students develop it through deliberate classroom practices.
Because most students' passions are nascent, the first task is helping them distinguish things they like from interests worth cultivating into long-term passions.
A forty-second private affirmation of a student's witnessed strength is presented as a high-leverage move that can help a student find purpose.
He distinguishes fruitful curiosity, acted on in ways that deepen mastery, from fruitless curiosity that comes and goes unexplored.
Grit is counted as only half a motivational strength because passion supplies the motivation while persistence is its product.
quotes: Sure, they have things they really like to do — riding dirt bikes, playing video games, reading novels — but these strong affinities are really just the seeds of the kind of passion that makes a person persist at something for the long term. The trick, then, is in helping our students identify which of their affinities may be worth developing into true, “I really have a hard time not thinking about this” passions.

I think it borders on magic. It's magic because it makes us (teachers) better, more affirming human beings; it's magic because it takes 40 seconds of work and can yield 40 years of results (another example of small time investments yielding huge returns); and it's magic because it can help a student discover a purpose for themselves.
Carry around an index card and write questions that occur to you throughout the day. At day's end, spend 10 minutes exploring a question or two using the Internet or a textbook.

Use any extra minutes at the end of a lesson to have students ask you great questions. I love saying to my students, “Okay guys, three minutes to make me earn my pay: ask me some hard questions about today's [reading, lesson, etc.]!

Passion is the motivational element — passion makes teachers stick to it, and artists, and engineers, and parents, and priests, and social workers. Persistence, on the other hand, isn't motivation — it's the product of motivation. Gritty people use passion to produce persistence toward long-term ends.
